notes:
I've built these notes from the pages I could read: Enduring Word (Guzik), the Pulpit Commentary, the Expositor's Bible, the Bible Hub and StudyLight verse pages (which include Ellicott, Gill, Barnes, Benson, Wesley, Cambridge and Keil & Delitzsch), Precept Austin, bible.org (Utley) and Bible Odyssey. Where a point is only quoted inside another page (for example Kidner or Yamauchi inside Guzik), I say so.

**Gaps:** I couldn't fetch Ellicott's or Gill's full chapter pages, so their views appear only in short pieces on verse pages. I found nothing from newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org or netbible.org, and no prosperity or word-of-faith teaching on this chapter. Those parts are left out.

---

**v. 1:** Pulpit says Darius "gave an order" rather than a formal decree. It reads "the house of the rolls" as a royal record room, used to store both documents and precious metals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm
- Benson says the search began in Babylon. When the edict wasn't found there, they searched Ecbatana. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/6-1.htm
- Barnes compares a record room found at Nineveh in 1850, whose floor was covered more than a foot deep in baked clay tablets. He thinks Babylon's was probably similar. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/6-1.htm

**v. 2:** Guzik says the search needed real persistence, and he sees God's hand in its not being abandoned. He cites Morgan on this. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/
- Guzik quotes Yamauchi, who cites de Vaux: Persian kings wintered in Babylon and spent summers in Susa or Ecbatana, and a forger in Palestine could hardly have been so accurate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/
- Pulpit says "Achmetha" is Ecbatana, not a "coffer" as some older readings had it. It describes the famous Median palace there and says Persian records were kept on parchment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm

**v. 3:** Pulpit links the order to lay firm foundations with Isaiah 44:28. It also judges the 60-by-60 cubit size unlikely to have been actually built. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm
- Guzik prefers Poole's view: the figures were upper limits set by Cyrus, not the actual plan. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/
- The Expositor's Bible suggests the height may include the terrace the temple stood on, or that the building never reached the permitted size. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/ezra/6.htm
- Utley thinks chapter 1 may give the spoken decree and chapter 6 the written archive copy. Ryrie says these extra details belong to an official memo, not a public announcement. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-6-commentary
- Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey): the Hebrew Bible doesn't describe the rebuilt temple beyond this verse's measurements. Its emphasis is that the temple stand exactly where the first one stood. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/the-destruction-and-reconstruction-of-the-temple/
- Pulpit's sermon notes treat the "foundations" as a picture of Christ, the foundation of the church. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-6.html

**v. 4:** Guzik quotes Kidner: the "great stones" that had made the officials suspicious (5:8) turn out to be expressly allowed. Guzik suggests the layering of stone and timber may have guarded against earthquakes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/
- Pulpit notes the Greek translation (Septuagint) read the phrase as storeys, though no known building used that pattern. It also points out that the Jews themselves paid large sums (2:69; 3:7), so the royal funding was either not carried out or covered only materials. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm

**v. 5:** Guzik calls it a remarkable providence that so many of the temple vessels survived intact and were sent back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/

**v. 6:** Pulpit thinks the writer shortened Darius's letter, keeping only its essential parts. "Be far from thence" means don't go near the Jews to trouble them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm

**v. 7:** Gill suggests Darius may have had some hint that the officials meant to cause trouble. Keil & Delitzsch see a special emphasis on the elders. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/6-7.htm
- Guzik says Darius saw, as the elders did, that the temple had to stand on its old foundations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/

**v. 8:** Pulpit says the expenses came out of the tribute the province already owed, with only the balance sent to the court, so taxpayers carried no extra burden. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm
- Guzik reads it differently: like a typical politician, Darius put the cost on the province rather than his own treasury. He sees God turning the opposition of 5:3 into help for the work (Romans 8:28). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/

**v. 9:** Pulpit explains these animals were Israel's main sacrifices, and the wheat, salt, wine and oil went with the grain offerings that accompanied every burnt offering. Supplies came "day by day" because sacrifice was offered daily. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm

**v. 10:** Pulpit notes that Jews have long prayed for the rulers of the lands they lived in, and that Persia gave special honour to the royal house. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm
- Guzik says wanting these prayers was part of Darius's motive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/
- A sermon on Precept Austin calls it Darius covering his bases, which God used to provide for His people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-6-commentary

**v. 11:** Pulpit says changing a Persian decree was an extremely serious crime (compare Daniel 6:8), and believes crucifixion is meant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm
- Guzik notes that Adam Clarke weighs flogging, hanging or impaling. He quotes Yamauchi that Darius impaled 3,000 Babylonians. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/
- Gill pictures a gallows made from a beam of the man's house, and the house pulled down and never rebuilt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/6-11.htm
- The Expositor's Bible allows for exaggerated Eastern language. It also says this is a kind of state support for religion "which no one would defend in the present day," though it notes the Jews had only asked to be left alone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/ezra/6.htm

**v. 12:** Benson says Darius was struck by the greatness of Israel's God. Gill reads "caused His name to dwell" as God's presence, the Shechinah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/6-12.htm
- Guzik and Meyer apply Proverbs 21:1: the king's heart is in the Lord's hand. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/

**v. 13:** Pulpit says Tattenai and his colleagues had no hostility toward the Jews, and their goodwill partly explains how quickly the temple was finished. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm
- Guzik quotes Kidner on possible political motives, such as keeping order on the route to Egypt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/

**v. 14:** Guzik says God's blessing didn't make the work easy; it still needed the prophets' encouragement. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/
- **Why "Artaxerxes" is named.** Pulpit rules out Xerxes and identifies him as the later Artaxerxes, who ordered the temple "beautified" (7:20, 27). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm
- Kidner (quoted by Guzik) says the name was added to complete the picture, "whether by the author or by an early scribe." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/
- Kretzmann (Lutheran) says Artaxerxes is named for the gifts he sent with Ezra. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/ezra-6.html
- Utley says Artaxerxes' decree concerned the city walls. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-6-commentary
- Matthew Henry says the elders were shamed into the work by the zeal of these pagan kings. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Ezr/Ezr_006.cfm
- Precept Austin notes the same word, "decree," is used for both God and the kings: God's decree stands behind theirs. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-6-commentary

**v. 15:** Pulpit counts 21 years from the foundation, and four years, five months and ten days from the restart (Haggai 1:15). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm
- Barnes dates it to 516–515 BC. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/6-15.htm
- The Bible Hub study note sees exactly seventy years from 586 BC, fulfilling Jeremiah. https://biblehub.com/ezra/6-15.htm
- Bible Odyssey says most scholars date completion to 516/515 BC. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/the-destruction-and-reconstruction-of-the-temple/

**v. 16:** Pulpit notes the writer calls the returnees "Israel," not just "Judah," and links the new temple with the old. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm
- Guzik quotes Kidner: the word for dedication, *hanukka*, later named the feast of John 10:22. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/

**v. 17:** Guzik compares these 712 animals with Solomon's roughly 142,000, saying the smaller gift may have been more beautiful to God. He quotes Kidner that the twelve goats confessed failure but also faith that all twelve tribes were one people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/
- Pulpit says God accepts what we have, and that Christ, "the Messenger of the covenant" (Malachi 3:1), later gave this temple greater glory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm

**v. 18:** Precept Austin uses this verse as an example of worship ordered by Scripture, as part of "the joy of purity and obedience." https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-6-commentary

**v. 19:** Pulpit: the fourteenth was the day set by Moses' law (Exodus 12:6). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm
- Henry says that before this, disturbances and lack of room had kept them from celebrating with proper solemnity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Ezr/Ezr_006.cfm

**v. 20:** Pulpit, Barnes and Cambridge read the verse as a contrast: the priests had purified themselves, but the Levites were "all pure, as one man," so the Levites killed the lambs even for the priests. Cambridge traces how the duty moved from household heads to Levites (Hezekiah, Josiah). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/6-20.htm
- Utley sees an emphasis on the people's unity. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezra-6

**v. 21:** This is the main interpretive split in the chapter. It falls between individual commentators rather than neatly along denominational lines.
- **Converts from paganism.** Gill (Baptist) says these were circumcised converts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/6-21.html
- Clarke (Methodist) sees converts won by the exiles' example in Babylon. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/6-21.html
- Benson (Methodist) agrees, and with Matthew Henry makes them a picture of converts welcomed to the "gospel feast." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezra/6-21.html
- Pulpit, Poole and JFB take the same view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/6-21.htm
- **Israelites who never went into exile.** Ellicott (Anglican) says they were the Jewish remnant who had mixed with the foreign settlers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/6-21.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch and Cambridge also say Israelites, arguing from parallel passages. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/6-21.htm
- Hole agrees, citing Jeremiah 52:16. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbh/ezra-6.html

**v. 22:** Guzik quotes Adeney: calling Darius "king of Assyria" is an old way of naming the ruler of former Assyrian lands, which supports the account's authenticity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-6/
- Pulpit also gives a view where "the king" means the lord of Western Asia in general, now Israel's friend instead of her oppressor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezra/6.htm
- Precept Austin calls the title unusual. It also links the feasts to the Lord's Supper, "Christ our Passover." https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-6-commentary
- A Maclaren sermon on the verse says God means His children to be glad, and joy that doesn't come from Him is false. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/6-22.htm
